source_text: Homilia in illud: Ego vado ad patrem meum Κυρίλλου ἐπισκόπου Ἱεροσολύμων εἰς τὸ "Ἐγὼ πορεύομαι πρὸς τὸν πατέρα μου· καὶ ὃ ἐὰν αἰτήσητε ἐν τῷ ὀνόματί μου, τοῦτο ποιήσω, ἵνα δοξασθῇ ὁ πατὴρ ἐν τῷ υἱῷ". Ἐπ' ἀμφοτέρων τῶν περὶ τῆς θεότητος καὶ τῆς ἀνθρωπότητος λεγομένων τίθησιν τὸ ἐγώ, ὡς τὴν μὲν διάνοιαν τῶν ῥημάτων ἐκ τῆς ἀκολουθίας φαίνεσθαι, τὴν δὲ διάγνωσιν τῶν φύσεων ἐκ τῆς διαφορᾶς τῶν λεγομένων. ἐκ δὲ τοῦ διαλέγεσθαι ἐν ἀμφοτέραις ὡσὰν περὶ ἑνός τινος τὴν τοῦ προσώπου συνάφειαν σημαίνει.
orientation: Cyril of Jerusalem opens his homily by quoting the Gospel saying of Christ, “I am going to my Father…,” and then states how the pronoun “I” functions in it.
pass_a_gloss: Homily on that saying: I go to my Father. Of Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem, on the saying “I am going to my Father; and whatever you ask in my name, this I will do, so that the Father may be glorified in the Son.” In the case of both the things said about the divinity and the humanity, he places the “I,” so that the meaning of the words is shown from the context, but the distinction of the natures is shown from the difference of the things said. And from his speaking in both cases as though about a single person, he signifies the union of the person.

bible_refs.note: The homily quotes the saying in a form close to the Greek Gospel text: “I am going to my Father; and whatever you ask in my name, this I will do, so that the Father may be glorified in the Son.”

pass_b_english: A homily by Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem, on the text, “I am going to my Father; and whatever you ask in my name, this I will do, so that the Father may be glorified in the Son” (John 14:12–13). In the statements made about both his divinity and his humanity, Christ places the “I,” so that the meaning of the words is shown by their context, while the distinction of the natures is shown by the difference in what is said. And because he speaks in both cases as though about a single person, he signifies the union of the person.
